Do you think there should be fewer distros? Do you think some should be combined? Why are new distro's a 'bad' thing?
Discussion: is linux weakened or strengthened by the vast selection of distributions?

Too much choice can be overwhelming at times for a new user like myself. Studies actually suggest that the more choice you have, the more critical and uncertain you are about your decision. But, since distros are free it's not a big deal. I find that having options is worth the minimal frustration involved in finding a distribution you're happy with.

There really aren't that many distros strictly speaking. What you're seeing is many flavors each composed of a smaller subset of Linux base versions (Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, etc.)

I'm enjoying having a wide variety of flavors available so one can try multiple GUIs without hashing out driver issues each time as the core itself hasn't changed..

Well they all offer different things and I think that's a good thing. You have ultra-stable distros like Slack and Debian, to high-security like Tails and Qubes, to bleeding edge like (my personal favorite) Arch. It gives you choice on what you want.

The few main distros appeal to different types of users and the their needs. I guess the same can be said of all the forks but most of them are much more need specific. I think about the only thing missing is a truly unified package manager.

I like the fact that i can grab a distro for a specific purpose that will require very little configuration to do what i need it to.

Weakened. Duplicated dev\test effort alone has wasted so much time it's insane. Plus all the different distro's each with unique and different problems scare off the new users. And don't get me started on the religulous fanatics...
Define weakened or strengthened. Usability? Number of users? Security? I feel like it's a bit of a vague question. Each could be debated all day. I'm using Mint now FWIW

I mean, it is really a weakness, and a strength at the same time. Yes, intimidating, and possibly distressing when shit like the systemd debate shows up for new user threads. However, trialling different distros, finding the right branch that does what you want to do, how you want to do it, is part of the new user experience. It is that first step in questioning what your OS does. If you decide to go arch, you have your reasons, and they are good ones. Just like if you go mint, or slackware, or gentoo, or [insert you favourite here]. And it has never been as easy with booting off a usb key, or demoing in a virtual machine.

The only reason why new distro's are a "bad thing", is maybe due to the fact that there is a non-zero chance that what it attempts to do is done better with more experienced coders on an older distribution, or that it is being attempted just for the sake of it, which let's be honest, if it gets people involved on some level, and furthers someone's own knowledge base, I am all for it. Or they do something like the Remix OS where it gets shady.
Weakened. Half-baked distributions create headaches for new users. Aside from that, duplication of efforts is a huge resource waste in the open source world.

Choice is a good thing, but it can also be overwhelming for new Users. The Linux Sucks guy makes a great point about how forking is creating a mess of various linux projects, a relatively new example being OpenSSL and LibreSSL.

That said, I would rather be overwhelmed with choice (as a soon to be new Linux user myself), than to be told what I can install and have no decision beyond pressing Next, in the matter. :)

The duplication of effort is immense. There are millions of wasted man-hours every year. Every university student has a "me-too" project and all of them believe they can do better than anyone else while putting in quarter of the effort.
The amount of distributions is fine, and has never been the problem. The problem has always been getting people to work together, disregarding what project you work on, even if it's not a distro.
It weakens Linux because there are some good ones, but there are a lot more shit ones that don't need to exist.
How do you decide they dont need to exist? Are there people who use them? Are they dedicated to them? Does the distro serve a specific purpose?
Because no one will use them. A lot of them are depreciated too, like Zorin.
And some are completely abandoned in favor of a paid version, like Parted Magic. I still use it regularly.

Having the truly unique distros is nice. I mean the ones that have different package managers, set ups, and a slightly different philosophy on the community should be managed. It allows people to explore the different ideas and try things out until they find something that they're comfortable with, or you can study how they work and try building your own.

Strengthened!

If all of them were starting over from scratch, then Linux as a whole would be weakened, because man hours would be applied to fix the same problems over and over again.

Instead, the problems are solved and the software is assembled in a billion parts. Then the distribution carriers put together distributions with all those parts. Finally, other distributions build on those distributions.

Most famous example: The folks over at Debian collected all the parts for a good distribution. Ubuntu takes the Debian system and adds more up-to-date software pieces and more custom software. The people at Linux Mint make a version of Ubuntu that does a better job of respecting privacy and also uses a different desktop environment. Then there is Xubuntu, Lubuntu, etc. etc. These guys are all just taking the Ubuntu distribution and swapping out the DEs.

So, we get lots of different flavors of Debian. No individual working group is reinventing the wheel, they are just offering different configurations for our personal taste.
